scenes.line1: How does Go run so many tasks?
scenes.say: Ever wonder how Go runs thousands of tasks at once without breaking a sweat? What's the secret sauce behind Go's famous concurrency?

scenes.label: Goroutine
scenes.sub: A lightweight thread managed by Go's runtime
scenes.say: Meet the goroutine. It's a super lightweight thread, managed entirely by Go's runtime, not the operating system.

rows.b: Thousands run on few OS threads

scenes.say: Here's how it works. You start a goroutine, and Go's scheduler takes care of the rest. It multiplexes thousands of goroutines onto just a few operating system threads, handling blocking and input output so your app keeps humming.

scenes.code:
ch := make(chan int)
go func() { ch <- 42 }()
value := <-ch
scenes.say: But how do these goroutines talk? With channels. You can send and receive values safely between goroutines, like passing a message in a bottle.

scenes.label: Select
scenes.sub: Wait on multiple channels at once
scenes.say: Need to juggle multiple channels? Use the select statement. It lets you wait on several channel operations at the same time.

scenes.question: Can goroutines leak if not cancelled?
scenes.right: Yes! Always signal cancellation with context
scenes.say: Here's a common trap: thinking goroutines always clean themselves up. Not true! If you don't signal cancellation, you can leak goroutines and waste resources. Use context to avoid this.
